passages.where: A song of ascents, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. In Hebrew a house meant a household as well as a building, so the builders here include parents. Rising early and staying up late cannot do what only the LORD does, and he gives sleep to those he loves.

Moses gives Israel the heart of the law: the LORD is one, and he is to be loved with everything. The words are to be on the parents' own hearts first. Only then are they taught, and they are taught in ordinary places: at home, on the road, at bedtime and at breakfast.

In a Roman household the father held legal power over his children as long as he lived, and harsh discipline was common. Paul tells children to obey, and then puts a limit on the father that ordinary household rules did not: do not provoke your children to anger.

Ancient writers on the household spoke to the head of the house about managing his dependents. Paul speaks to children directly, as people responsible to the Lord, and gives fathers a duty with a reason: a child who is constantly provoked loses heart.

Isaac loves Esau and Rebekah loves Jacob. The Bible sets down the favoritism without comment, and the next chapters show what grows from it: a deception, a stolen blessing, and a brother who wants to kill his brother.

Mary and Joseph are a full day's travel home from Passover before they notice that the twelve-year-old Jesus is not with them, and they search three days. Mary's words are a rebuke full of fear. Even the parents of Jesus did not understand him at once, and Luke says he went home with them and grew.

Jesus is teaching his disciples to pray. He points to something every parent in the crowd knew: no father hands a hungry son a snake instead of a fish. Parents who are themselves sinful still know how to give good things, and the Father in heaven gives more.

Isaiah announces that God is coming to his exiled people as a mighty king. In the same breath he describes him as a shepherd who carries the lambs and gently leads the ewes that are nursing their young. The strength of God and his gentleness with the weary are one.

Paul reminds a young church how he cared for them, and he reaches for the pictures of a nursing mother and a father. The father's work, as he describes it, is encouraging, comforting and urging, with the goal of a life worthy of God.

The disciples try to keep children away from Jesus, as if they were an interruption. Jesus is indignant, the only time the Gospels use that word of him, and he says the kingdom belongs to such as these. He takes them in his arms and blesses them.

misread.taken: This verse, often remembered as “spare the rod, spoil the child” (a saying that is not in the Bible), has been used to justify punishment given in anger, and harm that leaves marks, as a parent's religious duty.
misread.says: The proverb's target is the parent who never corrects at all, which it calls a failure of love. It assumes a parent who loves the child and aims at the child's good, not a parent venting frustration. The word for rod also names a shepherd's staff and a ruler's scepter, and Proverbs uses it of correcting adult fools as well as sons. Faithful Christians differ on whether the verse speaks of physical discipline (see below), but no reading of it permits injury or abuse, which the whole Bible condemns, and it must be read beside the command not to provoke children (Ephesians 6:4).

misread.taken: The “quiver full” of verse 5 is used to rank families: the more children, the more blessed and faithful the parents, and the smaller or childless home falls short.
misread.says: The psalm calls children a heritage, a gift handed down, not a wage earned. In its world, grown sons were a household's protection, the people who stood beside their father when he faced opponents at the city gate where disputes were settled. The psalm praises children as God's gift; it does not measure anyone's faith by their number, and Scripture honors those who have no children, among them Jesus himself.

whole: Parenting struggles come in every size. A toddler who will not sleep, a ten-year-old who lies, a teenager who has gone silent, a child with needs nobody prepared you for, or simply the exhaustion of doing it day after day with too little help. Underneath most of them sits the same fear: that you are getting it wrong, and that your child will pay for it. Christian parents often add a second weight, the sense that a godly home should look calmer than theirs does.

The Bible is more honest about families than most parenting advice. Its homes are full of trouble: Isaac and Rebekah each with a favorite, Eli unable to restrain his sons, David's household torn apart, and Mary and Joseph searching three days for a son they did not understand. Scripture does not present a model family to copy. It presents a God who keeps working through families that are not models, and who calls himself a Father who gives good gifts even to children who have not earned them.

What the Bible asks of parents is smaller and harder than a method. The words are to be on your own heart first; children learn faith mostly from what they watch, at the table and on the road, before they learn it from what they are told. Discipline is real and necessary, and Proverbs has no patience for the parent who never corrects. But the New Testament adds, twice, the command that parents in Paul's world did not expect to hear: do not provoke your children, or they will lose heart. Correction that comes from a parent's anger or pride teaches a child something other than wisdom.

That leaves room for grace in both directions. Parents will fail, sometimes in ways their children remember for years, and the path forward is the ordinary one of the Christian life: confess it, ask forgiveness, including from the child, and keep going. The psalm says that unless the LORD builds the house, the builders labor in vain. That is not a reason to stop building. It is permission to sleep, and to remember that the child belongs to God before they belong to you.

differ.share: Christians agree that children are a gift from God and bearers of his image, that parents are called to teach and correct them in love, that no discipline may harm or abuse a child, and that a child's faith is finally God's work.

views.name: Measured physical discipline
views.body: Many Christians read Proverbs 13:24, with 22:15, 23:13-14 and 29:15, as endorsing measured physical discipline for young children, given calmly, privately and in love, never in anger, and always with the aim of the child's good. They note that the proverb's point is that withholding correction is a failure of love.

views.name: Discipline without the rod
views.body: Other Christians hold that the rod in Proverbs stands for correction in general, since the same book uses it of adult fools, and that Proverbs describes the methods of its own culture rather than a technique for every age. They discipline through consequences, instruction and close relationship, often citing the command not to provoke children (Ephesians 6:4, Colossians 3:21).

views.name: Children and baptism
views.body: Christians also differ on the place of children in the church. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptize the infants of believers as members of the covenant community; Baptist and many other churches dedicate infants and baptize on a person's own profession of faith.

differ.after: All of them call parents to love, patience, instruction and correction without harm, and all of them pray for their children's faith as something only God can give.

sit: What do your children see in you on an ordinary Tuesday that teaches them what you actually believe about God?

prayer.lead: A prayer of Moses that asks for God's work to be seen by the next generation, and for the work of tired hands to last.
